modules.label: Personality
modules.instructions: Describe yourself as you generally are now, across your life, rather than only at work. Choose how accurately each statement describes you. There are no right or wrong answers. You may skip a statement.
modules.attribution: International Personality Item Pool (IPIP). Public-domain items; IPIP-NEO-120 developed by John A. Johnson.

modules.label: Work interests
modules.instructions:
What would you enjoy doing at your dream job?

In the next section, you’ll read 30 work activity descriptions that some people do on their jobs.

Read each one carefully and try to picture yourself doing that activity.

Decide how much you’d like to do the activity. Tap or click on one of these answers:
Strongly Dislike · Dislike · Unsure · Like · Strongly Like

Do not think about the amount of education needed or how much money you’ll make (that will come later).

This is not a test! There are no right or wrong answers!
modules.attribution: This page includes information from the O*NET Career Exploration Tools by the U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (USDOL/ETA). Used under the CC BY-ND 4.0 license. O*NET® is a trademark of USDOL/ETA.

modules.label: Personal values
modules.instructions: Here we briefly describe some people. Please read each description and think about how much each person is or is not like you. Using a 6-point scale from “not like me at all” to “very much like me,” choose how similar the person is to you.
modules.attribution: Sandy, C. J., Gosling, S. D., Schwartz, S. H., & Koelkebeck, T. (2016, published online). The development and validation of brief and ultrabrief measures of values. Journal of Personality Assessment. https://doi.org/10.1080/00223891.2016.1231115

modules.label: Type preferences — research version
modules.instructions: Describe your usual preferences as you generally are now, across your life, when you have reasonable freedom to choose. Report what you tend to prefer, not what you are skilled at, what your job requires, or what sounds admirable. Different situations may bring out different preferences. Use the midpoint when a statement is neither accurate nor inaccurate; you may skip any statement. These items concern preferences, not ability, intelligence, kindness, or mental health.
modules.attribution: Original candidate wording prepared for this project on 2026-09-22. Not copied from MBTI, OJTS, Insights, True Colors, Color Code, or DiSC assessment items. This is not a validated assessment.
modules.source: Original draft in this research kit; broad construct references S05 and methods references S23-S26.

big5.reverseKey: For key -1, keyedValue = 6 - answer; for key +1, keyedValue = answer.
big5.computation: Sum and arithmetic mean of keyed values, only when every item in that scale is answered. keyedResponseCounts lists counts for keyed values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
big5.interpretation: Self-reported tendencies, not ability, diagnosis, moral worth, or population rank. The response midpoint is 3; no norms or population percentiles are supplied.

interests.computation: keyedValue = answer - 1. Each interest sum adds its five keyed values. originalResponseMean = sum / 5 + 1. All thirty items must be answered before any interest score is shown.
interests.interpretation: Appeal of work activities, not competence or a career-fit score. A sum of 10 is the response midpoint; it is not a population average. Ties do not identify a unique leading interest.

values.computation: After all twenty answers: grandMean is their arithmetic mean; rawMean is the mean of each value pair; centered = rawMean - grandMean. The equivalent integer-numerator calculation is (10 * pairSum - totalOfTwenty) / 20.
values.interpretation: Relative priorities within this person. Above zero means above their own overall endorsement mean, below zero means below that mean, and zero means equal to it. Not a moral grade, absence of a value, or between-person norm. The ten centered scores sum to zero and are not independent.

domains.name: Openness to Experience
domains.definition: Openness describes engagement with imagination, ideas, art, feelings, and unfamiliar experiences. It is not intelligence or technical aptitude.

domains.name: Conscientiousness
domains.definition: Conscientiousness describes self-reported preparation, organization, persistence, responsibility, and deliberation. It does not measure moral worth or the quality of your code.

domains.name: Extraversion
domains.definition: Extraversion includes social approach, assertiveness, activity, excitement, and positive emotion. It is broader than talkativeness and does not measure leadership potential.

domains.name: Agreeableness
domains.definition: Agreeableness describes trust, consideration, cooperation, and interpersonal approach. Agreement is not the same as kindness, and disagreement is not a personal failing.

domains.name: Neuroticism
domains.definition: Neuroticism describes self-reported negative emotion and reactions to stress. Higher scores mean more endorsement of these experiences; this is not a clinical diagnosis.

facets.name: Artistic Interests
facets.definition: Interest in art and aesthetic experience.

facets.name: Adventurousness
facets.definition: Preference for variety and unfamiliar experiences.

facets.name: Intellect
facets.definition: Interest in abstract and challenging ideas. This is not an IQ score.

facets.name: Liberalism
facets.definition: Responses to the original political and values statements. Cultural meaning can vary; this does not establish political identity.

facets.name: Self-Efficacy
facets.definition: Confidence in handling tasks successfully. This is self-report, not a skills test.

facets.name: Self-Discipline
facets.definition: Preparation, starting, and carrying out plans.

facets.name: Friendliness
facets.definition: Ease and warmth in approaching people.

facets.name: Gregariousness
facets.definition: Preference for being around groups of people.

facets.name: Morality
facets.definition: Responses about using or obstructing others. The historical label “Morality” is not an overall moral grade.

facets.name: Altruism
facets.definition: Interest in helping and attending to others.

facets.name: Cooperation
facets.definition: Responses about interpersonal conflict and retaliation.

facets.name: Modesty
facets.definition: Self-presentation and self-regard. Modesty is not ability or worth.

facets.name: Depression
facets.definition: Low mood and negative self-evaluation. This historical label is not a depression diagnosis.

facets.name: Self-Consciousness
facets.definition: Discomfort drawing attention in social situations.

scores.name: Enterprising
scores.definition: Influencing, organizing, or leading toward a goal.

scores.name: Conventional
scores.definition: Working with organized information and procedures.

scores.name: Conformity
scores.definition: Avoiding actions that upset or harm others and meeting shared expectations.

scores.name: Tradition
scores.definition: Respecting inherited practices, beliefs, and customs.

scores.name: Benevolence
scores.definition: Caring for the welfare of people close to you.

scores.name: Universalism
scores.definition: Concern for people broadly and for the natural world.

scores.name: Power
scores.definition: Influence, status, and control over resources.
